A tsunami of genome reshuffling
abstract: Generation-by-generation ancestry tracking in hybrid stickleback shows that hybrid incompatibilities drive rapid removal of introgressed alleles following a tsunami.

title: Rapid genome-wide purging following tsunami-induced hybridization in a stickleback population
abstract: Speciation is the process by which barriers to gene flow evolve between populations. As speciation approaches completion, genome-wide divergence can be maintained in the face of hybridization. Because real-time observations of genomic changes following hybridization in natural populations remain rare, little is known about the processes and mechanisms by which introgressed genomes are purged in nature. Here we report a 9-year genomic monitoring of a tsunami-induced hybrid stickleback population, revealing rapid genome-wide purging within only a few generations. On 11 March 2011, a devastating tsunami struck the Tohoku Region, Japan, creating new stickleback habitats and inducing hybridization between freshwater Gasterosteus aculeatus and marine Gasterosteus nipponicus . Within the first few generations, G. nipponicus alleles were purged at major loci responsible for reproductive isolation, including ancestral-X and neo-X chromosomes. These loci are involved in freshwater survival, migratory divergence associated with habitat choice, sexual isolation and hybrid sterility. Subsequently, G. nipponicus alleles were purged across the genome except at several loci. We provide direct evidence from a natural population that rapid genome-wide purging allows species identity to persist even after extensive introgression. Elucidating the genetic mechanisms underlying genome-wide purging is crucial for understanding the factors that drive progress towards speciation completion.

title: A microbial therapy-mimicry assay shows how spatial resource dynamics control resistance escape
abstract: The evolution of therapy resistance in structured populations such as biofilms and solid tumours is shaped by emergent spatial organization, with profound consequences for evolution-based therapies. However, how treatment reshapes these patterns remains poorly understood. Here we show that intermittent treatment pulses transiently reconfigure the resource landscape, reorganize spatial growth zones and can enable resistant mutants to escape spatial confinement and drive therapy failure. We introduce a spatial evolution assay in which populations expand from single, genetically tailored yeast cells, enabling quantitative tracking of the full spatiotemporal trajectories of continually emerging resistant mutants under intermittent treatment. By integrating these observations with a mechanistically interpretable computational model in a real-to-sim-to-real loop, we identify a dynamic phase-transition-like boundary in schedule space that defines a candidate optimal balance between population control and sustained resistance confinement, which we test experimentally. Together, our results establish resource-mediated spatial confinement as a central organizing principle of resistance evolution and provide a mechanistic foundation for spatially informed, evolution-based therapies.

title: Global sea-level rise will create a new biological invasion front
abstract: Climate change is causing a redistribution of life on Earth but also creating new habitats that can result in biological invasions. Despite great efforts focused on predicting range expansions of non-native species under climate change, its induced sea-level rise may open new habitats for the landward expansion of marine non-native species into inundated coastal lands, which remains unexplored. Here we show that over two-thirds of inundated coastal land area (approximately 290,000–470,000 km 2 ) will be environmentally suitable for 122 established non-native marine animals by the middle and end of this century, particularly in estuaries of mid-latitude regions. This emphasizes the need to consider sea-level rise when conducting invasion risk predictions under climate change scenarios. The development of effective early-warning systems and proactive management strategies will become critical for detecting and mitigating marine invasions into inundated regions as coastal lands continue to be reclaimed by the ocean across the world.

title: Development constrains the evolution of gene regulation after whole-genome duplication
abstract: Large-scale multiomics in two salmonids reveals that developmental and tissue-specific programmes dictate the evolutionary fate of duplicated gene expression and regulatory element activity after whole-genome duplication, with the vertebrate phylotypic stage representing the peak of regulatory constraint. Our study suggests that enhancers, transposons and conserved non-coding elements influence duplicate gene expression evolution.

title: Developmental contexts of gene-regulatory evolution following whole genome duplication in salmonids
abstract: Whole genome duplication (WGD) events during early vertebrate evolution may have promoted phenotypic innovation by expanding the genetic material for functional diversification. However, their ancient origins obscure how gene regulation evolved during rediploidization, the process that generates duplicate genes and regulatory elements following WGD. Salmonids provide a unique window to these mechanisms, because they experienced a more recent autotetraploid WGD and remain at an earlier stage of rediploidization. Here we generated 771 multiomics datasets spanning embryonic and adult tissues in Atlantic salmon and rainbow trout to investigate the evolution of gene expression and regulatory elements. Our analyses show that regulatory evolution following the salmonid WGD was shaped by developmental and tissue-specific constraints known to act across vertebrate species. We identify a peak of within-genome regulatory constraint at the vertebrate phylotypic period, associated with the functional retention of duplicated enhancer pairs harbouring deeply conserved non-coding elements enriched in motifs for master developmental transcription factors. We further identify roles for enhancers and transposable elements in the expression divergence of duplicated genes. This study advances the understanding of regulatory evolution following WGD and offers an open resource supporting vertebrate comparative genomics and research applications in salmonid aquaculture and conservation.

title: Global patterns in plant–pollinator specialization
abstract: Pollination is a key ecological process sustaining biodiversity and food security, yet global patterns of plant–pollinator specialization remain unresolved. Using a global dataset of quantitative plant–pollinator networks (>3,400 networks, >110,000 interactions), we show that specialization is latitudinally structured, but not as a single directional pattern. We find no consistent monotonic increase or decrease in specialization towards the Equator. Instead, network-level and pollinator specialization peak at low northern latitudes near the tropical–subtropical boundary, whereas plant specialization is hemispherically asymmetric. Climate is most often the best-supported predictor of specialization compared with latitude, biodiversity and environmental productivity. Network-level specialization declines with increasing mean annual temperature, with strong group-specific differences. Precipitation exerts nonlinear effects: plant specialization peaks at intermediate precipitation but is lower at the wettest sites, whereas pollinator specialization is lower at intermediate precipitation, although often in interaction with temperature. Pollinator groups diverge strongly, especially in contrasting precipitation-related patterns between birds and insects. These findings show that global plant–pollinator specialization is structured by latitude and climate in complex and taxon-specific ways, with implications for uneven responses of pollination networks to future climatic change.

title: An ancient evolutionary origin for IL-1 cytokines
abstract: Inflammation is widely considered a hallmark of animal immune responses. In mammals, this process is mediated in part by pro-inflammatory cytokines of the interleukin 1 (IL-1) superfamily, which establish and support microenvironments that regulate immune cell activity. However, the evolutionary origins of IL-1 cytokines remain elusive, as homologous proteins have been difficult to confidently identify outside vertebrates using sequence-based approaches. Although IL-1 family members have been described in all vertebrate lineages, including cartilaginous and jawless fishes, their distribution and evolutionary relationships beyond these groups remain unclear. Here we applied protein structure prediction algorithms to identify genes encoding a previously unrecognized family of IL-1 proteins (termed ‘IL-1anc’ to reflect their ancestral evolutionary origin) with homologues throughout Eumetazoa. Here, using Petromyzon marinus (sea lamprey) and Strongylocentrotus purpuratus (purple sea urchin) as model systems, we demonstrate that IL-1anc proteins share key features with mammalian IL-1α/IL-1β, including expression patterns, subcellular localization and post-translational processing. Together with previous evidence identifying other IL-1 axis components in invertebrates, our data support a model in which the IL-1 superfamily and associated circuitry represent a foundational module of animal immunity that far predates the jawed vertebrates.

title: Avian migration timing advances linked to season-dependent population benefits
abstract: While migratory species can adjust their migration timing in response to climate change, it remains unclear whether these shifts can insulate them from population decline. Here we compiled a global database pairing 4,351 population-level estimates of migration timing across 549 avian species with corresponding population trends and rates of climate change at breeding and non-breeding grounds, coupled with a full-annual-cycle theoretical model. Building on evidence for an accelerating advancement in bird migration over the past century (cumulatively advanced 13.86 days from 1970 to 2019), we show that rapidly advancing migration is beneficial for bird abundance during pre-breeding migration but detrimental during post-breeding migration. The net demographic benefit depends on pre-breeding advancement outpacing that during post-breeding migration. This benefit is more pronounced in large-bodied species. Our findings highlight that population benefits of rapidly shifted migratory behaviour are season dependent, underscoring the importance of full-annual-cycle perspectives for understanding and conserving migratory species under global change.

title: Unifying bright spots research for people and nature
abstract: Understanding how systems thrive against the odds is increasingly important in an era of accelerating ecological and social change. Bright spots, cases that outperform expectations under local constraints, offer a lens for learning from success within broader patterns of decline. Yet progress in this field has been limited by inconsistent definitions, fragmented methods and the absence of an integrative framework for systematic learning and application. Here we synthesize more than 70 studies spanning ecology, conservation, resource use, food production and sustainability science to assess how bright spots are identified, interpreted and applied in research, policy and practice. We introduce a typology of six approaches for identifying bright spots, highlighting their assumptions, strengths and trade-offs. We distil enabling conditions associated with bright spots, grouped into specific practices and processes, social capacities and context. Building on this synthesis, we develop a unifying framework that moves bright spots research from isolated case studies towards a coherent and cumulative understanding of how unexpected success can be identified, interpreted and compared across systems. By uncovering conditions under which systems exceed expectations, bright spots research reveals where unexpected success happens, why, and how to replicate it in an era of accelerating social–ecological change.

title: Interaction matrices as unifying tools for navigating ecological complexity
abstract: Interaction matrices summarize pairwise species impacts within ecological communities into an analytically tractable format. Despite their contribution to linking subdisciplines and advancing our understanding of ecosystem dynamics, they have faced recurring criticism for oversimplifying ecological complexity. Extensions developed to address specific shortcomings often come with trade-offs, including increased data demands and analytical complexity. Here we review the foundations of the interaction matrix framework and examine the state of the art of approaches developed to tackle its challenges. We argue that the unifying role of interaction matrices could be improved by embracing, rather than fighting, their inherent nature as uncertain and transient abstractions. We explore how such an approach could bring substantial benefits and incorporate advances from wider complexity sciences. As we enter the second century of interaction matrices within ecology, such a shift will reinforce their place as a valuable tool to unlock the complex dynamics of ecological communities.

title: Biodiversity safeguards ecosystem services and functions worldwide
abstract: Biodiversity loss threatens ecosystem services on which humanity depends, yet the strength, form and context-dependency of biodiversity–ecosystem service and biodiversity–ecosystem function relationships remain poorly quantified. Here we synthesize 423 studies to determine how biodiversity affects ecosystem functioning and service delivery. We show that regulating services, including water quality and pollination, often exhibit linear relationships, suggesting an additive role for diversity. While biodiversity enhances most functions and services, our effect-size analysis shows that oceanic ‘blue carbon’ sequestration is exceptionally sensitive, revealing how critical marine biodiversity is for climate mitigation. Conversely, services such as hazard regulation appear relatively insensitive to biodiversity, instead depending on a few functionally unique foundational species whose persistence nonetheless is interdependent on the wider community. Our new synthesis enables the forecasting of impacts, for example, that biodiversity loss will reduce pest regulation in countries experiencing population growth and intensive development, and it also highlights how ecosystem services might be used to anticipate future problems.

title: Combining conservation strategies
More biodiversity means stronger, more reliable ecosystem functioning worldwide
abstract: A global synthesis reveals that biodiversity is a major driver of ecosystem functioning and service delivery, and that biodiversity loss is likely to have widespread effects on people and ecosystems.

title: Dispersal diversity buffers species vulnerability to local extinction
abstract: Predicting species persistence within ecological communities is a fundamental challenge for both empirical and theoretical ecology. Existing methods span from mechanistic models, whose parameters are difficult to estimate from data, to statistical tools whose context-specific parameters are less interpretable. Here we present a general framework, grounded in the statistical physics of complex systems, that integrates the key processes governing species survival into a single measurable quantity: the competitive balance. This metric quantifies the vulnerability of a focal species to competitive exclusion beyond what is captured by its abundance alone by incorporating the diversity of dispersal strategies and the structure of interspecific interactions within the community. Crucially, the competitive balance can be inferred from spatial abundance data, thus circumventing the need to estimate species traits or dispersal parameters. Our results reveal that greater heterogeneity in dispersal strategies reduces vulnerability to competitive exclusion for a given abundance. We validate the framework using tropical and temperate forest data and discuss how it can be applied to a range of different ecosystems, providing a systemic and interpretable tool for assessing a context-dependent species vulnerability that accounts for its interactions with the entire community.

title: A science-driven agenda is needed to implement China’s National Parks Law
abstract: China’s new National Parks Law marks a clear shift from fragmented protected-area governance to a unified, legally binding conservation framework that operates at a national scale. Its success will depend on how well scientific evidence is integrated into its implementation; progress is needed in climate-adaptive planning, monitoring, and community-based governance to ensure that its legal ambition delivers lasting ecological benefits.

title: Three ways that international financial architecture reform matters for biodiversity
abstract: Achieving Global Biodiversity Framework targets will require addressing not only the direct drivers of biodiversity loss but also the global financial rules that shape them. We argue that the current international financial architecture reinforces extractive development pathways, constrains investment in ecological transition, and limits ambitious environmental policy, which makes financial system reform an essential component of the transformative change needed for biodiversity protection.

title: Pale pavement plumage
Biodiversity enhances pond ecosystem multifunctionality across Europe
abstract: Small water bodies, such as ponds, are crucial for biodiversity and support multiple ecosystem functions (multifunctionality). Yet, the extent to which their biodiversity contributes to multifunctionality remains largely unexplored. Here we report data from a large-scale, highly standardized, stratified field survey across 206 European ponds, including 2,500 observations of biodiversity (macrophytes, zooplankton, macroinvertebrates and amphibians) and key ecosystem functions and processes, including methane emissions, litter decomposition, carbon sequestration, primary productivity, biomass accumulation and habitat complexity. Our study reveals a positive and significant association between biodiversity and multifunctionality across multiple taxonomic groups of aquatic organisms, with several ecosystem functions strongly linked to zooplankton richness. The biodiversity–ecosystem multifunctionality relationship tended to be more pronounced in arid regions. By contrast, increasing nutrient concentrations associated with intensive cropland (that is, eutrophication) were negatively related to multiple ecosystem functions, underscoring the importance of pond ecological status in supporting multifunctionality. Taken together, our work provides evidence of the importance of biodiversity in maintaining multifunctionality in small standing freshwater bodies. Preserving and restoring pond habitats by reducing nutrient concentrations will sustain key ecosystem functions in the face of multiple drivers of biodiversity loss.

title: Bumblebee hotspot
Patchy global progress to nature recovery
abstract: The Kunming-Montreal Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF), adopted in December 2022, sets out a mission for nations to “take urgent action to halt and reverse biodiversity loss to put nature on a path to recovery”. A report presenting a midway review of its 23 action targets and 4 goals, to be met by 2030 and 2050, respectively, will be published in October 2027. We spoke to Flavio Affinito, co-author of the report and technical expert on the KMGBF monitoring framework, and Emily Nicholson, co-chair of the Ad Hoc Scientific and Technical Advisory Group for the report.

title: Didactic dicynodont
Countries not on track to halt nature loss
abstract: The complexity of achieving the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework vision of living in harmony with nature is becoming only more apparent as nations show their first cards on progress.

title: The kinetic basis of photosynthetic heat tolerance
abstract: Photosynthetic heat tolerance constrains primary productivity and defines the upper temperature limit of the biosphere. However, current approaches to heat tolerance either overlook the duration of heat exposure or describe temperature–time relationships without characterizing causal mechanisms, constraining hypothesis testing and prediction under novel conditions. Heat inactivation of photosynthesis has been posited to result from protein denaturation or lipid membrane breakdown, but their relative contributions are not well resolved. Here we develop and test a quantitative theory of photosynthetic heat inactivation based on chemical kinetics and use the theory to evaluate these competing mechanisms. By analysing photosystem II temperature responses in 177 plant species from 157 families, we show that protein denaturation, not lipid membrane breakdown, governs heat tolerance. The theory also predicts an upper acclimatization limit of ~60 °C, set by the thermal stability of heat shock proteins and supported by global data for 826 species. Our findings provide a predictive, mechanistic basis for photosynthetic heat tolerance and the thermal limits of the biosphere in a changing climate.

title: Drift, selection and recombination bias drive the evolution of a non-ribosomal peptide
abstract: Non-ribosomal peptides play important roles in microbial ecology and medicine, for example as toxins and antibiotics such as penicillin. Like ordinary proteins, non-ribosomal peptides are subject to evolutionary change, which is driven by rampant recombinations of their synthetases. The evolutionary dynamics and causes of non-ribosomal peptide diversification are not well understood, because recombinations complicate phylogenetic analysis and statistical tests for natural selection and drift. Here we study the non-ribosomal GameXPeptides, which entomopathogenic bacteria use to kill their insect prey. We use recombination-aware phylogenetics, ancestral sequence reconstruction and statistical analysis of historical recombination patterns to retrace the evolution of GameXPeptides. This uncovers dozens of new GameXPeptides, including striking patterns of structural convergence. We provide statistical and experimental evidence that this diversity is shaped by selection, but also that GameXPeptides experience substantial genetic drift and biased recombination rates that limit the space of accessible peptide variants. Our work illuminates the complex interplay of adaptive and non-adaptive evolutionary forces acting on some of the most versatile chemical weapons in nature.

title: Soil viruses as key regulators of the microbial carbon pump in deep soils
abstract: Deep soils store over half of terrestrial organic carbon, yet the viral mechanisms governing carbon persistence in subsurface contexts remain unclear. Here, by conducting a soil profile survey (0–700 cm) across four agroecosystems and a global synthesis of subsurface metagenomes, we established the Deep Soil Viral Resources Database, comprising 50,949 viral operational taxonomic units and 3,902 auxiliary metabolic genes (AMGs). Viral richness increased significantly with depth, accompanied by a shift towards lysogeny driven by declining carbon availability. The deep-soil virome carried AMGs and lysozymes involved in polymer degradation and cell endolysis. Viral endolysin significantly promoted necromass carbon accumulation, which contributed to increases in mineral-associated organic carbon. A synthesis of 138 global soil profiles further revealed a positive effect of viral abundance on soil organic carbon. Our findings establish a framework where viruses strengthen the microbial carbon pump in deep soils by facilitating host carbon scavenging via AMGs and promoting necromass formation via endolysin activity.

title: Grazing cements kelp collapse
Tiny ciliate introns
Protecting the deep ocean under mining threat by connecting existing reserves
abstract: Modelling larval dispersal pathways reveals that protected deep-sea areas lack sufficient connectivity to replenish one another. The addition of strategically placed protected corridors linking the existing areas would protect current larval dispersal pathways and improve biodiversity conservation capacity in abyssal ecosystems that face mining threats.

title: Dispersal corridors enhance modelled near-bed larval connectivity across deep-sea protected area networks
abstract: The Clarion–Clipperton Zone (CCZ) is the focal region for imminent deep-sea nodule mining, with over 1.1 million square kilometres already under exploration licence. Although the International Seabed Authority has designated Areas of Particular Environmental Interest (APEIs) to protect regional biodiversity from mining impacts, there has been no formal assessment of whether this network functions as a coherent connected system. Here we use Lagrangian dispersal modelling and network analysis to provide a region-wide assessment of modelled larval connectivity across the CCZ and show that simulated larval exchange among APEIs is extremely limited. Under physically driven near-bed dispersal and reasonable pelagic larval dispersal times of 19–69 days, fewer than 0.02% of particles reach another APEI, with inter-APEI gaps exceeding modelled dispersal capacity. CCZ-wide dispersal is structured into four semi-isolated connectivity communities, and under mining disturbance when self-supply is removed from Areas of Mining Interest, unprotected non-mining areas emerge as the dominant modelled source of replenishment. Strategic corridor additions increase inter-APEI dispersal 406-fold and nearly doubles modelled replenishment from protected areas under disturbance, providing a reproducible, connectivity-informed evidence base for conservation design ahead of commercial mining.

title: Other effective area-based conservation measures may enhance global conservation networks
abstract: Other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs) are expected to have a crucial role in achieving the global ambition to protect 30% of the planet by 2030. While the number of OECMs is growing rapidly, their contribution to systems of conservation areas remains unclear. Here, to fill this gap, we developed a typology of the structural roles OECMs can play in conservation networks—enlarging, connecting, buffering and aggregating protected areas (PAs), and quantified their contributions using spatial data for 6,234 OECMs reported across 14 countries. We found nearly one-third of OECMs directly adjoin and enlarge PAs, while a smaller subset (~3%) connect or buffer isolated PAs or aggregate fragmented PAs. Although OECMs currently make limited contributions to increasing connectivity, two-thirds of OECMs lie less than 10 km from a PA, providing opportunities to consolidate conservation networks in the future. Our analysis provides a global assessment of how OECMs strengthen conservation networks and offers simple, policy-relevant insights into how to maximize the benefits of area-based conservation as countries pursue the 30 × 30 target.

title: A fully marine stem amphibian from the Late Triassic of China
abstract: Land vertebrates colonized the sea repeatedly through geologic time with various levels of marine adaptation, from partial use of marine resources to fully marine lifestyles. Mammals, reptiles and birds all have species that survive without food or fresh water from land; however, amphibians, including both crown and stem species, lack such a member partly because of their salt-intolerant skins. Here we report the first fully marine species of a stem amphibian, Gerrothorax maritimus n. sp., based on two nearly complete skeletons from the Late Triassic (about 237 million years ago). Its articulated occurrence far from land, together with associated strontium isotope record, suggests life in fully marine regimes. It descended from a lineage with complete body armour, which would limit skin-based water, gas or salt exchanges typical of amphibians and instead enforced the use of the gill and gut that can become more tolerant of salt—this probably prepared them for marine adaptation.

title: A mid-Cretaceous island as a cradle of Southeast Asian plant biodiversity
abstract: The renowned tropical flora of Southeast Asia is often regarded as being of relatively recent (Cenozoic) origin. Here, based on specimens embedded in mid-Cretaceous amber obtained from Kachin, Myanmar, we report on a large assemblage of exceptionally well-preserved plant fossils encompassing a rich diversity of angiosperms, together with many other seed plants and cryptogams. The morphospecies richness and clade diversity of this flora are among the highest recorded for any single Early to mid-Cretaceous plant megafossil assemblage. This ancient flora reached Southeast Asia rafted on the West Burma Block, an arc-shaped microplate that separated from the northwestern corner of the Australian Plate during the Jurassic and drifted north, finally colliding with Sundaland by the Eocene. The Burma Terrane remained low lying and at low latitudes in the intervening 100–50-million-year period, providing a sanctuary for clade preservation, a cradle for modern clade diversification and a conduit for transferring flourishing Gondwanan angiosperm lineages to Asia. These findings provide insight into the cradle of what ultimately became Southeast Asian angiosperm-dominated tropical forests, whose origins date back over 100 million years.

title: Temporal links in avian migration schedules across the annual cycle
abstract: Each year, migratory birds move thousands of kilometres across international borders to track optimal environmental conditions. How tightly annual-cycle events are linked and how much flexibility exists in migration schedules will determine how vulnerable migratory birds are to environmental change. Using a global tracking database, we reconstructed full annual-cycle schedules of 2,324 individuals from 83 species. We found strong temporal links during autumn and spring migrations: departure from the breeding grounds predicted arrival at the non-breeding grounds and vice versa. During both migration periods, late-departing individuals shortened migration duration, but still arrived later than early-departing individuals. By contrast, arrival at and departure from the non-breeding grounds were not correlated, suggesting a temporal reset that buffered earlier delays. Despite resetting during the non-breeding period, migratory schedules remain globally interconnected, such that disruptions in one season can propagate to subsequent stages of the annual cycle, with consequences for migratory species and the ecosystem functions they support.

title: Maternal inheritance accelerates sex chromosome degeneration and mitonuclear coevolution in a brood parasitic bird
abstract: The coevolution of interacting mitochondrial and nuclear genes is increasingly recognized as a critical component of organismal fitness and a potential source of genetic incompatibilities that promote speciation. In species with ‘ZW’ sex chromosomes, however, selection on maternally inherited traits may impact mitonuclear coevolution owing to the effective linkage of the W chromosome and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). Here we show that in brood parasitic cuckoo finches ( Anomalospiza imberbis ), enhanced ecological selection on a maternally inherited trait (mimetic egg colouration) subjects both the W chromosome and mtDNA to increased accumulation of slightly deleterious mutations via genetic hitchhiking, accelerating W chromosome pseudogenization and gene loss, as well as mitonuclear coevolution. Remarkably, as other W-linked genes were lost, two egg colour genes, representing likely targets of selection during cuckoo finch–host coevolution, were recruited to the W chromosome. Using structural models of the respiratory complexes and mitoribosome, we also show that the rate of amino acid substitution in nuclear-encoded residues is a function of their proximity to mtDNA-encoded residues, providing evidence of compensatory mitonuclear coevolution. Our results link species-level coevolution to both sex chromosome degeneration and mitonuclear coevolution. More generally, they highlight the genomic consequences of adaptation without recombination.

title: Non-ribosomal peptide diversity is driven by multiple evolutionary processes
abstract: Non-ribosomal peptides are microbial secondary metabolites that are synthesized by very large modular synthetase enzymes. Using a recombination-aware phylogenetic framework, we find that the evolution of these synthetases is driven by recombination and is subject to complex evolutionary forces.

title: OECMs contribute to strengthening existing networks of conservation areas
abstract: Our analysis provides a global assessment of the structural configuration of conservation networks that comprise both protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs), offering new insight into how OECMs are strengthening current protected area networks.

title: A risk framework for addressing nature’s harmful contributions to people
abstract: Conserving Earth’s ecosystems is critical for sustaining human life, yet some aspects of living nature can harm people, such as insect vectors of human disease and venomous animals. Nature’s contributions to people (NCPs) that cause harm are a contentious issue in biodiversity research and policy, with limited agreement on how they should be assessed or managed. We therefore propose a new conceptual framework for assessing and managing harmful NCPs that draws parallels with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s concept of climate risk. We argue that the risks of harmful NCPs should be understood as arising from the intersection of the hazardous aspects of ecosystems (ecosystem hazards) with societal exposure and vulnerability. Our risk-based approach equips decision-makers with a framework to systematically identify solutions for avoiding societal harms, while preventing maladaptive interventions that can undermine sustainability goals and degrade ecosystems. We conclude by outlining priority next steps for operationalizing our framework.
